pages.text: Acids are a cornerstone of modern chemistry, enabling a wide variety of reactions. Two very important industrial acids are sulfuric acid and hydrochloric acid, which we will both synthesize here.

pages.title: Sulfuric Acid
pages.text: There are two ways to synthesize sulfuric acid: the iron sulfide process and the contact process [TODO]. The iron sulfide process can be used to get a small amount of sulfuric acid, but is impractical at an industrial scale, unlike the contact process. However that needs sulfuric acid to begin with.

pages.title: Iron Sulfide Process
pages.text: To make your first batch of sulfuric acid, grind down an iron ingot and blend it with blaze powder. Smelting the blend will yield a clump of dirty iron sulfide, which can be dissolved in water, and the solution can then be distilled to get a little bit of sulfuric acid.

pages.title: Hydrochloric Acid
pages.text: Rock salt can be found on the seabed as white patches. Hydrochloric acid can be made from it in a Mannheim kiln [TODO], or, at a smaller scale, in a cauldron: dissolve it in cold sulfuric acid, with a water block above it to catch the HCl gas. Beware, as HCl gas can cause serious chemical burns!

pages.title: Making Hydrogen
pages.text: Hydrogen gas is necessary for hydrogenation reactions. You can obtain hydrogen gas by electrolyzing water [TODO], or, for now, by just tossing an iron ingot in a cauldron of sulfuric acid below the cauldron where the hydrogenation takes place.
